newsitem.title: UK: UK government, opposition trade "cheat' accusations.
newsitem.headline: UK government, opposition trade "cheat' accusations.

text.p: Parliamentary relations between Britain's ruling Conservative party and the opposition worsened when Labour angrily rejected accusations of cheating in order to win a House of Commons vote.
Labour's parliamentary business manager Donald Dewar denounced Conservative claims that he cynically engineered the defeat of the government as "simply an organised deception".
"It is totally without justification, and I really must put on record that I deplore that charge...and I think it does reflect enormously badly on those involved," he told a news conference.
The government defeat, by seven votes, was on a minor amendment to a bill designed to make "stalking". or harassing people by obsessively following them around, a criminal offence.
The government immediately claimed that 14 Labour MPs had voted despite having promised their Conservative "pairs" they would not do so.
"Pairing" is a parliamentary arrangement by which MPs on different sides agree mutually not to vote in a division, usually because one of them is ill or has a prior engagement.

Dewar and Archy Kirkwood, his counterpart from the minority Liberal Democrats, announced on Tuesday that they would suspend pairing after parliament returns from its Christmas recess after the Conservatives allegedly cheated in a key vote on Monday.
They discovered that three Conservative MPs had been "paired" with legislators from both their parties in a vote on fishing policy, artificially boosting the government's majority.
"We will certainly not be pairing when we come back in January," Dewar said.
He said he had checked with 11 of the 14 MPs named by the Conservatives and in no case had they "broken their pairs".

The absence of pairing when the Commons returns on January 13 from its Christmas break will make it still more difficult for the government to remain in office until May, when Prime Minister John Major must call a general election.

The government will be in constant danger of defeat in Commons votes and MPs face late night sessions to enable it to get legislation through. With the Conservatives over 20 points behind Labour in the opinion polls, Major is desperate to avoid an early general election.
